name: Mass Production

claims.claim_text: For weight- and size-constrained products headed to volume, laying a custom board with only the required circuitry beats carrying a general-purpose dev platform into the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't use a bloody Arduino. You go out and lay your own board and use, you know, and do the minimal amount of circuitry required to actually get the job done.
claims.episode_title: The Hard Work Hypothesis

claims.claim_text: A retail price is a rough upper bound on volume build cost: a $50 consumer touchscreen Wi-Fi appliance implies roughly $10 to $15 of volume cost to embed that same interface into another product.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if you can buy that retail for $50, imagine how much the cost is. You know, what is it, $10, $15 or something like that in volume to build a touchscreen Internet interface into something.
claims.episode_title: The Innovation Speculation

claims.claim_text: Volume price breaks are not linear; the halving seen going from one unit to a hundred does not repeat at a thousand units unless the design uses generic jellybean parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't just assume that when you go to a thousand units, your price is going to plummet to one tenth, because it may not.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: Distributor pricing contains anomalies where a quantity break is quoted higher than the single-unit price, so quoted breaks must be checked rather than assumed monotonic.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll see weird pricing anomalies too, where the quantity pricing is, is higher than the single unit.
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: Part selection should be made against large-volume pricing from the start, even when only a handful of units are planned near term, because the economics of volume manufacturing constrain the design itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: you really should be looking at those large volume prices anyway, even if you're just planning on building a couple of them for now
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: Hardware accelerators emerged that funded small teams roughly $15,000 to $20,000 to relocate to China and drive an idea to a mass production run within a couple of months.
claims.quote_verbatim: they want to give hardware companies $15,000 to $20,000 to come spend some time in China and work from their idea to a mass production run in a couple of months.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Tesla illustrates that building working prototypes and building the same vehicle at volume are separate problems, and the volume problem nearly ended the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: They could make their prototypes, no problems, but mass manufacturing almost killed them.
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Injection mold tooling around $50,000 per mold is a dominant line item that can consume most of a small hardware company's seed funding on the way out of 3D printed parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: and then you pay for molds at 50,000 bucks a pop or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: On mature silicon processes such as 180 nm, die area matters less when performance is obtained by paralleling many identical structures across a very high unit count.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, you don't, because they just parallel everything up, right? They just manufacture a million of them and parallel it up.
claims.episode_title: DIP projects, OSHW & Trade Booths - Demonstrative DIP Dacrygelosis

claims.claim_text: Factories that advertise no minimum order quantity are rare; the prevailing model is low non-recurring engineering charges recovered through margin on sustained volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: No. You know, we almost never find that model. So, the factories often will charge very low NRE or non-reoccurring engineering.
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Factories bid engineering effort up front and select programs expected to run for many years, because their return comes from improved margin in the later production years.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they really want to make their money on the volume. So, they want to look for something that's going to last over multiple years. And they can invest their engineering up front.
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware forces a promised delivery date of roughly three months because a realistic one-to-two-year manufacturing schedule will not attract backers.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to set some reasonable delivery date before you
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Handing an impossible schedule and a pre-sales budget to a team that has never manufactured anything at volume is structurally set up to fail regardless of the team's ability.
claims.quote_verbatim: taking a small group of entrepreneurs that have probably never built anything in volume in their lives, giving them an insanely short schedule
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Converting a solder-it-yourself kit into a volume product means redesigning it as a fully assembled, manufacturable unit rather than simply ordering more of the same parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: and kind of took it from the sort of kit based setup to a fully assembled, fully manufacturable design for mass manufacturing
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken Smith
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Choosing an off-the-shelf enclosure shifts engineering cost elsewhere, typically into internal wiring plus dedicated front and back panel boards to reach the connectors.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're maybe going to have to do some internal wiring, and you've got to design extra boards in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: 3D printed enclosures scale to roughly one to ten units and then stop; they are not a path into mass production.
claims.quote_verbatim: Try and put that into mass production. One of them, right? Yeah, one of them, maybe 10, you know, but then you're screwed for mass production.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: A designer with toy-industry mass-manufacturing background treats manufacturability of a novel consumer device as the settled part of the risk, leaving the software experience as the open question.
claims.quote_verbatim: with my background in toy design and mass manufacturing, that's kind of a given that we're going to be able to make it
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: For a consumer device combining optics, an ASIC and plastics, the plastics were judged the largest manufacturing risk, with schedule expected to be burned reconciling industrial design against manufacturability.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's the plastics by far. I fear that we're going to burn a lot of time in the first part of the year trying to compromise on the industrial design and something that's manufacturable.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Letting industrial design lead unchecked produces shapes with fancy compound curves that cannot be mass produced, a failure pattern observed at more than one company.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was the industrial designers were ruling the design. And I could see that they were coming up with stuff that wasn't going to be mass producible. Super fancy curves and everything.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: A thousand units of a wearable can be built essentially by hand, but sixty thousand units requires a completely different manufacturing plan.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a whole different game plan from going for manufacturing a thousand watches, which you can almost, you know, do, you know, almost by hand, um, to doing 60 odd thousand
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: After venture funding fell through, a watch team abandoned the plan to go overseas for full mass production and instead scaled up a local California prototype shop.
claims.quote_verbatim: We think that we could pull off, um, local at home manufacturing, not literally in our garage, but we, um, we had a, we had a prototype shop that we worked with, um, here in California.
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing-experienced reviewers can spot impossible production claims in funding campaigns, such as machining 400,000 pieces in two or three days at a cent apiece.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're going to machine 400,000 pieces in like two or three days. So we're cool.
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Reaching mass production on the first PCB spin is achievable, and was reported for several customers building wireless designs from vendor reference designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've had several customers go to mass production with their first spin of the PCB
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: A marginal timing error does not stay theoretical in production; it materializes as a pile of thousands of dead boards traceable to the responsible engineer.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you missed a timing, it's going to lay there and, you know, there's going to be a pile of 20,000 of them with your name on it.
claims.speaker: Bil Herd
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: Deliberately violating design rules is survivable only when the violation is engineered to hold across the part variation and process spread of mass production.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to make sure that what we did do, even when we broke the rules, that we did it in a way that would still work at mass production
claims.speaker: Bil Herd
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: A business selling modules under $10 survives on unit volume rather than per-unit margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: You got to sell a lot of them. Um, yeah. You're right. Volume. That's how we make it.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: Hardware development in practice is iterative rather than fully specified up front: assumptions get made, tried, and corrected faster than they can be reasoned out in advance.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's sort of this iterative design process by which you make a bunch of assumptions. And you just have to try stuff.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: A contract manufacturer may quietly hand-solder a part or work around a bad footprint to deliver prototype boards, hiding a defect that only blocks the order once volume is requested.
claims.quote_verbatim: it turns out that no, they sort of like hand soldered that part or they did this or they did that just to get the job done.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: The distinguishing feature of a good contract manufacturer is volunteering manufacturability feedback rather than silently building what was sent.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it's amazingly hard to get that kind of feedback. And I think that's what really separates a good contract manufacturer from a bad one.
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Some volume behaviors cannot be predicted from smaller builds, so the only real verification that a design works at a hundred thousand units is building a hundred thousand units.
claims.quote_verbatim: I really do feel like the only way to know if this is going to work when you build a hundred thousand is to build a hundred thousand
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Offshore knitting factories quote roughly one dollar per unit for 5,000 identical acrylic scarves, with the minimum order and single-material constraint being the real barrier rather than price.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want 5,000 of exactly the same scarf in acrylic, no wool, no nice cotton, no nice materials, just acrylic. I can order those for a dollar a scarf.
claims.speaker: Fabienne Serriere
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Fabienne Serrière of KnitYak

claims.claim_text: In volume production the line never pauses, so a discovered bug accrues defective units by the hour and forces same-day containment decisions.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're in volume manufacturing, you're building things constantly. And so, if you find a bug, every day matters. Every hour matters.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: The count of things that can go wrong grows with build quantity, which is why volume programs push engineers toward paranoid attention to detail.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're building anything at scale, the number of things that can go wrong just keeps going up and up
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: A build of a hundred units typically draws all of a given part from a single reel, so components behave nearly identically and mask any sensitivity to part spread.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you build 100 of something, chances are all those transistors came from the same reel.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: At high volume a design consumes many reels of each component, so parameters such as transistor threshold voltage shift from build to build in ways never seen in the lab.
claims.quote_verbatim: But when you go into the big volumes, things change. And you're going through reels of components. And so, you're seeing shifts in everything. You know, threshold voltage, everything.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: A design overly sensitive to component spread can stop working entirely when a reel arrives at the high end of a parameter the designer implicitly assumed was low.
claims.quote_verbatim: a bad design is going to be super sensitive and could actually stop working when you get a reel that's got a, you know, super high threshold voltage
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Second-sourcing a component widens the parameter spread the circuit must tolerate, because two suppliers' parts differ from each other as well as within their own distributions.
claims.quote_verbatim: Or you get a second source component and all of a sudden it's varying, you know, quite a bit because you've got two different suppliers.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Monte Carlo and simulation coverage of component variation is routine at the chip level but rarely available for every board-level part, so board designs must instead carry deliberate margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of it was taken care of in just doing simulations and Monte Carlo analysis and things like that. But, you know, you don't always get to do that on everything.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Design trade-offs chosen during prototyping stay unvalidated until a large build exercises them, which is when the accumulated assumptions are finally confirmed or exposed.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not until you actually try to build a large quantity that you actually get to validate that, you know, yeah, that was a good idea.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Consumer products must hold their operating margin across the environments customers actually use them in, with temperature the leading Monte Carlo parameter down to well below freezing.
claims.quote_verbatim: Temperature would be a big one. Because you're working on a consumer product, right? So, it could be used in some unheated hut in Norway somewhere at, you know, minus five degrees.
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Standing up a PCB assembly line for a consumer product took six separate trips to a factory near Shanghai across one year, beginning with early trial builds before volume work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually spent several weeks in China this year over the course of, I think I was there six times.
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Line bring-up starts with engineering trial builds well before volume, with the express purpose of getting the assembly line itself ready rather than producing sellable units.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it was basically for the purposes of setting up a PCB assembly line. And so, I went over sort of early in the year to kind of get ready and do some EV kind of trial builds
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: A defect discovered after thousands of boards are built converts into mass rework, including hand re-soldering of 0201-size passives.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's all fun and games until you find that there's a problem with those thousands. How do you guys feel about re-soldering 0201s by hand?
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: A consumer single-board computer is a reasonable choice for one-offs or about a hundred units, but not for a finished product built in thousands or tens of thousands.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would never recommend that someone put a Raspberry Pi into a finished goods project, right? A product, rather. If they're going to make, like, a one-off and they're going to make a hundred of something, you know, maybe.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Year End, 2017

claims.claim_text: The standard build ladder before volume is an engineering validation build (EVT), then one or more pre-production builds, then mass production.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll probably do a couple little builds, the EVT and then some pre-production and then you go into mass production.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: An EVT build uses production-intent hardware throughout, including real plastic tooling and real optical assemblies, so it exercises the actual manufacturing processes rather than prototype substitutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it was real plastic tooling with real circuit boards and real projectors and stuff like that in it.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Communications silicon programs commit to mass producing a fundamentally new technology before the end applications are fully defined, which drives much of the engineering difficulty.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're trying to build a completely different technology and mass produce it and put it into everybody's hand and sometimes the applications aren't even completely clear.
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: Shahriar Discusses 5G

claims.claim_text: Once a line is running at steady state, output flows smoothly because sophisticated factories carry heavy support infrastructure specifically to minimize and quickly recover from line-down events.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're actually in mass production, things flow pretty smoothly and yeah, I mean, lines go down, but the factories have, uh, a tremendous amount of like support and infrastructure in place to minimize that
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: The painful phase is ramp rather than steady state: climbing from one unit, to ten, to a hundred, to a thousand per day is where the process problems surface.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to build the first unit today. And then we're going to build 10 tomorrow and then a hundred the next day. And then a thousand the next day. Like when you're going through that process, that is excruciatingly painful.
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Boards built only for personal and experimental use avoid the certification burden, including FCC ID and RoHS compliance, that attaches to any mass-produced product.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's no Rojas. There's no FCC ID. I don't mass produce them.
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Optimizing a design for the fewest components while relying on free samples ignores part cost, so making the same tool mass producible required a ground-up redesign around different priorities.
claims.quote_verbatim: my design was made to use as few components as possible, but I didn't consider the price of the parts if they could be sampled.
claims.speaker: Travis Goodspeed
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Engineers moving from industrial or automotive work into consumer products over-specify protection and margin until they internalize that unit cost, not robustness, sets the design budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: well, they're over-designed things. It's like, no, no, no. Cost is the driver here.
claims.speaker: Ken Burns
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: United States government small-business research programs run in phases, with awards from tens of thousands up to over $200,000, a short proof of concept, a roughly two-year development phase, and a final phase aimed at mass production.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's awards range from tens of thousands over $200,000. And it's like a short proof of concept. And then there's like a two-year period, like a longer. And then finally, phase three is like actually making it in mass production.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hipster Fodder

claims.claim_text: Research-lab training teaches design against functional requirements with cost as a secondary concern, which does not transfer to volume products where cost is a primary driving function.
claims.quote_verbatim: I learned to design products based on functional requirements. And while cost was important, it wasn't as much of a driving function.
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: At a million units, shaving ten cents off the bill of materials returns $100,000, which reframes tedious part substitutions as fully funding additional headcount.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're producing a million units and you can save 10 cents on your bill of materials, while 10 cents doesn't seem like worth the time it took you to find that part or make the design change, that's a hundred thousand dollars you just saved.
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Volume cost reduction extends beyond part price to assembly economics, including qualifying unknown suppliers and reworking a circuit to cut the number of placements the pick-and-place machine must make.
claims.quote_verbatim: you put two resistors in the place of one because it, you know, like you're costing down total number of placements on a machine sort of thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Design for manufacturability on programs running hundreds of thousands of units starts during early research and development and consists largely of unglamorous compromises, such as enlarging features so they can be probed and tested.
claims.quote_verbatim: Some of our projects in like the hundreds of thousands of units being manufactured now. And we were doing it all the way from early R and D. So lots of, lots of boring compromises you have to make when you go to production.
claims.episode_title: Reunion Impedance Matching and 2023 Predictions

claims.claim_text: Working inside a manufacturer that ships thousands of units teaches the gap between building one of something and building a hundred thousand, a lesson difficult to acquire from design work alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I learned a lot from just, uh, the difference of producing one thing and producing a hundred thousand of that.
claims.speaker: Carl Bugeja
claims.episode_title: Motors on PCBs with Carl Bugeja

claims.claim_text: Wartime United States aircraft production reached roughly one B-17 bomber every 45 minutes, with the entire facility layout and supply chain planned without any computing assistance.
claims.quote_verbatim: back in World War II, the U.S. was cranking out B-17 bombers. A new bomber every 45 minutes or something like that.
claims.episode_title: Engineering Careers with Circuit Break & James Lewis

claims.claim_text: The early automotive assembly line marked the shift from hand-fitting parts in one-off batches to interchangeable parts built to tolerance, the same assumption electronics manufacturing now takes for granted.
claims.quote_verbatim: going from hand fitting everything and having to hand make everything and one off batches to now we are going to try to build an assembly line to just build something that's interchangeable parts
claims.episode_title: Engineering Careers with Circuit Break & James Lewis

claims.claim_text: Every packaged microcontroller die is individually tested after wafer sawing and packaging, and the resulting test data stream is monitored continuously as the primary production quality signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: every chip is tested, right? So every time you saw your wafer up, you put it in, uh, in its package, uh, and then you, then you put it in a tester and it does a ton of tests on each chip to make sure that the chip's good.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Beyond per-die testing, mature chip production runs periodic package qualification to confirm that packaging materials have not begun to introduce reliability problems.
claims.quote_verbatim: you also do, uh, uh, what we call package qualification, uh, fairly regularly just to check that the, the kind of quality of the package, the materials aren't causing any issues
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: An older microcontroller is kept in full production maintenance mode alongside its successor because it remains slightly cheaper, which matters for extremely price-sensitive applications.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a teeny bit cheaper as well than 2350. So for super price sensitive applications, there's a cost saving there.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Off-the-shelf modules costing around twenty dollars now cover the early validation work that once required custom hardware, shortening the phase before a product commits to manufacturing.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's easier now because there are more modules that you can buy off the shelf.
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: A hundred thousand pre-orders forced an immediate jump from garage-built hardware to mass production, with a team that had never worked with a factory or visited China.
claims.quote_verbatim: We had a hundred thousand users or a hundred thousand customers right out, right off the bat. And so we knew that we had to shift from the hacker build it in the garage mentality to the, we need to build this in mass production.
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: Bringing that first volume build up meant relocating a team of seven or eight people, one per discipline, to live at the factory in China for six months.
claims.quote_verbatim: We flew to China, basically spent six months living there. We had a small team of seven people or eight people.
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: A six to twelve month build cycle before the first units reach customers means all program costs are carried up front with no revenue in return.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is tough when there's like a six to 12 month build cycle to get into the first people's hands
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

attribution_notes: ep=81 passage is labeled Dave Jones. Content splits across two voices: the warning about volume price breaks and the power-supply video series are Dave Jones (he made that video series), while the reply 'I think that as you're designing a product, you really should be looking at those large volume prices' is the other participant, so that claim is left null.
ep=87 passage is labeled Ian Danaher but the accelerator description reads as generic back-and-forth, so speaker is null.

ep=104 [4] is labeled Dave Jones; the Tesla manufacturing remarks alternate between both participants, so speaker is null. [5] uses 'in the end, folks' and the mold-cost figure, which matches Dave Jones, so he is named there.

ep=113 passages are labeled SPEAKER_01. The substantive answers about factory NRE/volume economics and crowdfunding schedules are the guest Scott Miller describing his own manufacturing-consulting work, so he is named.

ep=222 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE and labeled Chris Gammell, but the content is the guest recalling Commodore production floors ('a pile of 20,000 of them with your name on it'), so it is attributed to Bil Herd.
ep=226 quote spans the host's question and the guest's one-word answer, so speaker is null even though the answer is Colin Karpfinger's.

ep=229 [20] is labeled Dave Jones. The learner voice ('I wanted to solve it the other way', works with contract manufacturers, Valve-side experience) is Jeff Kaiser; the 'only trap with doing it that way' explanation about hand-soldered prototype parts is Dave Jones. The line about what separates a good contract manufacturer from a bad one sits at the handoff and is left null.
ep=257 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the scarf ordering economics are the guest describing her own sourcing, so Fabienne Serriere is named.

ep=279 [23] and [24] are labeled Chris Gammell, but the speaker describes designing the Valve controller and setting up a PCB assembly line in China, which is the guest Jeff Kaiser. The closing Norway/temperature line is the interviewer, left null, as is the 0201 rework quip in [24].
ep=437 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the factory-floor and ramp answers are the guest Chrissy Meyer describing her own consumer-hardware experience.
ep=442 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; both quotes are the guest describing his own boards, so Travis Goodspeed is named.
ep=458 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the cost-driver anecdote is the guest recounting his own employer, so Ken Burns is named.

ep=577 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; the SRI-to-startup narrative and the penny-per-unit arithmetic are the guest Michael Corr. The 'hardware engineers are cheapskates' aside with the placement-count example is the interviewer Chris Gammell.
ep=614 is labeled Dave Jones but the hundreds-of-thousands-of-units DFM work is the consulting guest speaking, so speaker is null.
ep=663 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE and labeled Dave Jones; the one-versus-hundred-thousand learning is the guest Carl Bugeja describing his prior employer.
